recipes.title: Plan a project on your desktop
recipes.description: Choose by scheduling depth, file interchange and whether a text-based model is useful. These local planners do not imply the collaboration features of their separate cloud products.

picks.label: Local Gantt planning
picks.reason: Task dependencies, baselines and resource-load views cover everyday individual scheduling.
picks.tradeoff: Shared editing requires a separate collaboration arrangement.

picks.label: Critical path and cost controls
picks.reason: Desktop combines critical-path analysis, work breakdown, baselines and earned-value views.
picks.tradeoff: Validate imported Microsoft Project files; portfolio features belong to a separate cloud product.

picks.label: Constraint-driven text models
picks.reason: Declarative schedules can account for resource constraints and be regenerated from versioned source.
picks.tradeoff: Learning the scheduling language takes more effort than dragging a bar on a chart.

recipes.title: Schedule people across projects
recipes.description: Distinguish calculated capacity-aware scheduling from a shared timeline. Start with the real constraints and test a representative plan.

picks.label: Shared resource planning
picks.reason: Portfolio planning and capacity allocation are central to its documented project controls.
picks.tradeoff: A configured server and an agreed project process are necessary.

picks.label: Reproducible capacity model
picks.reason: Resource constraints and scheduling rules can be expressed as reviewable text.
picks.tradeoff: Technical modeling is required and collaborative editing is external.

picks.label: Shared work-package plans
picks.reason: Dependencies, work packages and project discussions live in one team service.
picks.tradeoff: Do not assume every enterprise scheduling or portfolio feature is in Community.

recipes.title: Run a self-hosted product backlog
recipes.description: Pick the workflow first: Scrum ceremonies, cycles and product documents, or configurable issue states.

picks.label: Scrum and Kanban teams
picks.reason: Backlogs, sprints, stories and burndown views follow familiar agile planning workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Several services must be deployed and maintained.

picks.label: Cycles and product context
picks.reason: Cycles, modules and pages connect planned work with product documentation.
picks.tradeoff: Edition limits and operational requirements need review.

picks.label: Configurable issue workflows
picks.reason: Custom fields, role controls, wikis and repository integrations suit structured project tracking.
picks.tradeoff: Ruby deployment and plugin compatibility require technical ownership.

recipes.title: Host your own Kanban boards
recipes.description: Compare board scope and licensing before committing a team or inviting external clients.

picks.label: Focused WIP workflow
picks.reason: A compact board with work-in-progress limits and event actions suits a deliberate small workflow.
picks.tradeoff: The project is explicitly in maintenance mode.

picks.label: Imports and broad board features
picks.reason: Swimlanes, custom fields, rules and imports support richer board organization.
picks.tradeoff: Its larger feature and deployment surface needs administration.

picks.label: Real-time internal collaboration
picks.reason: Cards, comments and attachments provide a direct shared board experience.
picks.tradeoff: Community terms restrict some external commercial and hosted uses; check the exact license.

recipes.title: Track personal tasks and time locally
recipes.description: These tools cover different parts of a personal workflow; select a visual task tree, a terminal task list, or interval tracking.

picks.label: Desktop task trees
picks.reason: Nested tasks and effort records keep detailed personal work in a local GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Use current package instructions because older website release text is stale.

picks.label: Automated terminal tasks
picks.reason: Filters, reports and hooks integrate task lists with shell workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Command syntax replaces a visual planning interface.

picks.label: Tagged time intervals
picks.reason: CLI timers, backfill and reports complement a Taskwarrior workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Team approvals and invoicing are separate concerns.

picks.label: Visual time timeline
picks.reason: Editable intervals, tags and PDF/CSV reports suit a personal or freelance timesheet.
picks.tradeoff: Running the local web service still takes setup.

recipes.title: Choose a self-hosted business system
recipes.description: Define accounting localization, stock processes and implementation capacity before selecting a general ERP. The guide compares documented scope rather than certifying regulatory compliance.

picks.label: Integrated business operations
picks.reason: Accounting, purchasing, inventory and manufacturing are available in one Frappe-based suite.
picks.tradeoff: Implementation and localization are substantial work.

picks.label: Modular small-business workflows
picks.reason: ERP and CRM modules can be introduced around the processes a smaller organization needs.
picks.tradeoff: Specialized modules and hosted services may have separate costs.

picks.label: Modular ERP with desktop client
picks.reason: A native client and browser access share modular accounting, stock and manufacturing services.
picks.tradeoff: The desktop client still requires an administered Tryton server.

picks.label: Community application ecosystem
picks.reason: The LGPL Community edition provides a base for integrated business applications.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise-only modules and capabilities must be checked separately.

picks.label: Custom business foundations
picks.reason: A Java business framework supports teams developing their own operational applications.
picks.tradeoff: This is an implementation project, not a turnkey accounting download.

recipes.title: Manage parts, assets or expiring stock
recipes.description: Inventory software is specialized: components, assigned IT equipment and warehouse lots represent different records and transactions.

picks.label: Components and assemblies
picks.reason: Parts, BOMs, suppliers and build stock connect component availability to assembly work.
picks.tradeoff: Financial accounting and retail checkout are separate systems.

picks.label: Electronics bench inventory
picks.reason: Datasheets, component parameters, labels and KiCad integration suit electronic parts.
picks.tradeoff: External suppliers or AI services may have their own access and pricing terms.

picks.label: Assigned IT equipment
picks.reason: Check-in/check-out records show who holds equipment, licenses and accessories.
picks.tradeoff: It is an asset register rather than a warehouse fulfillment system.

picks.label: Lots and warehouse movements
picks.reason: Facilities, shipments, lot identifiers and expiry dates fit distribution workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Deployment and warehouse process training are required.

recipes.title: Choose a self-hosted CRM
recipes.description: Compare configurable business records, prebuilt sales/service processes and developer-defined applications.

picks.label: Sales and service processes
picks.reason: Contacts, opportunities, quotations and service records support an established CRM workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Review the current 8.x compatibility and migration documentation.

picks.label: Custom entities and fields
picks.reason: A configurable data model and REST interface adapt customer records to a particular business.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced extensions and cloud hosting can add fees.

picks.label: CRM applications as code
picks.reason: Custom objects, workflows, SDK and CLI tooling fit a developer-owned CRM implementation.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise files have commercial terms and customization needs technical ownership.

recipes.title: Issue invoices from your own server
recipes.description: Check the actual billing workflow, branding restrictions and local e-invoice obligations before moving customer data.

picks.label: Focused quotes and invoices
picks.reason: Customer records, templates, quotes and payment tracking cover a compact billing workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced automation and full accounting are outside its main scope.

picks.label: Recurring billing under MIT
picks.reason: Recurring invoices, contacts and payment links are available through a self-hosted application.
picks.tradeoff: Payment gateways and operational support have separate costs.

picks.label: Broader billing and client portal
picks.reason: Recurring invoices, expenses, payment gateways and desktop clients connect to a billing server.
picks.tradeoff: Elastic License restrictions and paid branding removal need review.

recipes.title: Keep small-business books under your control
recipes.description: Choose between an offline single-user program, a shared browser application and a larger ERP. Verify accounting localization against the business’s requirements.

picks.label: Offline single-user bookkeeping
picks.reason: The free desktop edition keeps accounting available without a subscription or network connection.
picks.tradeoff: Multi-user arrangements differ and the FSL includes a noncompete restriction.

picks.label: Self-hosted browser bookkeeping
picks.reason: The current Frappe application combines ledgers, invoices, stock and point-of-sale records.
picks.tradeoff: The previous Electron desktop application is end-of-life; the successor requires a server.

picks.label: Accounting within a full ERP
picks.reason: Financial records connect to purchasing, inventory and manufacturing workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Implementation effort is greater than a focused bookkeeping application.

recipes.title: Budget or account with local data
recipes.description: An envelope budget and a double-entry journal solve different problems; choose the data-entry model you will maintain consistently.

picks.label: Envelope budgeting
picks.reason: Local-first budgets and transaction imports support a planned allocation of personal spending.
picks.tradeoff: Bank-data integrations and hosted sync may incur separate costs.

picks.label: Versioned plain-text accounting
picks.reason: Text journals and scriptable reports make double-entry records inspectable and reproducible.
picks.tradeoff: Learning journal syntax and accounting rules takes commitment.

picks.label: Graphical double-entry accounts
picks.reason: A graphical accounting workflow is suitable when text journals are not the preferred entry method.
picks.tradeoff: Budgeting behavior differs from an envelope-first application.

recipes.title: Build internal business tools
recipes.description: Start with where the data lives and who maintains the tool: spreadsheet-style records, no-code databases or interfaces over existing services.

picks.label: Relational spreadsheets
picks.reason: Typed tables, Python formulas, linked views and access rules add structure to spreadsheet-style editing.
picks.tradeoff: Its relational document model differs from a conventional spreadsheet grid.

picks.label: No-code database applications
picks.reason: Tables, relationships, forms and an application builder support data-centered workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Premium and enterprise functionality have separate commercial licenses.

picks.label: Interfaces over existing systems
picks.reason: Widgets, database/API connectors and JavaScript build admin tools around current infrastructure.
picks.tradeoff: Queries, credentials and access controls require developer ownership.

recipes.title: Run a small-shop point of sale
recipes.description: Test the actual receipt printer, barcode reader, payment arrangement and local fiscal requirements before production use.

picks.label: Browser-based register
picks.reason: Item stock, customer records, receipts and sales reports can run on a local web server.
picks.tradeoff: Its MIT-derived license requires visible footer attribution, and peripherals need validation.

picks.label: Desktop till and back office
picks.reason: A desktop register with receipt layouts, barcode support and kitchen-display integration targets shop hardware.
picks.tradeoff: Recent maintenance was not established from the older release listing.

recipes.title: Choose a terminal workspace
recipes.description: Separate a terminal emulator from the shell it runs. Decide whether panes, remote sessions, configuration language or a minimal window matter most; GPU acceleration alone does not establish a performance winner.

picks.label: Integrated terminal workspace
picks.reason: Tabs, panes, multiplexing and Lua configuration support a multi-session terminal workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Its configuration and built-in session model take time to learn.

picks.label: Extensible Linux/macOS terminal
picks.reason: Kittens and keyboard-oriented terminal features support a configurable workstation.
picks.tradeoff: Native Windows support is not established.

picks.label: Platform-integrated terminal
picks.reason: Native desktop integration and terminal features suit supported macOS and Linux systems.
picks.tradeoff: Check platform feature differences and available package routes.

picks.label: Focused terminal window
picks.reason: A deliberately focused emulator works well with an external shell and multiplexer.
picks.tradeoff: Tabs and session management may require other tools.

recipes.title: Inspect and edit binary files
recipes.description: Choose between direct byte edits, reusable binary structures and a native desktop interface. Preserve an original copy before changing a file.

picks.label: Direct Windows hex editing
picks.reason: A Windows hex editor covers byte-level inspection and editing without requiring a template language.
picks.tradeoff: Structured parsing and cross-platform workflows need other choices.

picks.label: Reusable binary templates
picks.reason: Templates expose fields and structures in supported binary formats.
picks.tradeoff: It is commercial software and templates still require format knowledge.

picks.label: Pattern-driven binary analysis
picks.reason: A pattern language and visual analysis tools help inspect structured binary data.
picks.tradeoff: The broader analysis interface has a learning curve.

picks.label: Native macOS editor
picks.reason: A Mac-focused hex interface fits local inspection of large files.
picks.tradeoff: Its platform scope is macOS.

recipes.title: Choose a computational notebook workflow
recipes.description: Consider execution order, collaboration artifacts and the surrounding analysis workspace before choosing a notebook interface.

picks.label: Reactive Python notebooks
picks.reason: A dependency-aware execution model and Python source files help make state relationships explicit.
picks.tradeoff: Reactive behavior differs from a traditional manually executed notebook.

picks.label: Focused notebook interface
picks.reason: A familiar notebook document combines code, rich outputs and explanatory text.
picks.tradeoff: Execution state and cell order still require discipline.

picks.label: Larger analysis workspace
picks.reason: Notebooks, editors, terminals and extensions can share a workspace.
picks.tradeoff: Extensions and multiple tools increase environment-management work.

recipes.title: Choose a local SQL engine
recipes.description: Local transaction storage, file analytics and versioned relational tables are different needs. These tools overlap in SQL access but are not interchangeable database designs.

picks.label: Small local relational database
picks.reason: The CLI operates directly on SQLite files and can be scripted.
picks.tradeoff: SQLite concurrency and type behavior should fit the application.

picks.label: Analytical queries over local data
picks.reason: An in-process analytical engine suits SQL exploration of columnar and tabular files.
picks.tradeoff: It is not a replacement for every multi-user transactional service.

picks.label: Versioned relational data
picks.reason: Git-like table history supports branching and reviewing database changes.
picks.tradeoff: Its versioning and SQL compatibility require a representative trial.

recipes.title: Serve analytical or time-series data
recipes.description: Choose around query shape, ingestion, deployment scale and operational ownership. No common workload benchmark was run for this guide.

picks.label: General analytical service
picks.reason: A column-oriented database targets large analytical queries and aggregations.
picks.tradeoff: Running a shared service requires capacity, storage and upgrade planning.

picks.label: Timestamp-oriented ingestion
picks.reason: Its documented time-series features suit timestamped measurements and events.
picks.tradeoff: SQL and storage behavior differ from general-purpose transactional databases.

picks.label: Local analytical processing
picks.reason: An embedded engine can avoid operating a server for a single-user analytical task.
picks.tradeoff: A local embedded workflow does not provide the same shared-service architecture.

recipes.title: Browse databases with a GUI
recipes.description: Verify the actual database driver, authentication method and edition before choosing a client. A client does not replace the database service.

picks.label: Multiple database types
picks.reason: A database browser and query editor supports a mix of engines and local data work.
picks.tradeoff: Check each connector and any paid-edition feature requirements.

picks.label: Focused SQL desktop workflow
picks.reason: A query-and-table interface suits day-to-day SQL inspection.
picks.tradeoff: Community and commercial editions differ.

picks.label: Broad database ecosystem
picks.reason: Driver-based connections and data tools cover many database families.
picks.tradeoff: Its breadth creates more configuration and interface complexity.

recipes.title: Version database schema changes
recipes.description: Migration style, database support and current licensing matter more than the number of features on a product homepage. Test rollback and drift behavior on a representative schema.

picks.label: Plain SQL migrations
picks.reason: A compact CLI keeps migration files close to ordinary SQL.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced orchestration and governance need other systems.

picks.label: Ordered migration workflow
picks.reason: Versioned migrations fit a deployment pipeline with explicit sequence.
picks.tradeoff: Database coverage and advanced commands vary by edition.

picks.label: Structured changelogs
picks.reason: Changesets and changelog formats support explicit database-change history.
picks.tradeoff: Current Community uses FSL terms, and rollback is change-dependent.

picks.label: Desired-state schema planning
picks.reason: Declarative models can produce migration plans from a desired schema.
picks.tradeoff: Apache Community, standard binaries and Pro capabilities have different scope and terms.

recipes.title: Orchestrate data jobs
recipes.description: Compare the unit you want to manage: scheduled DAGs, Python flows, data assets or event-driven workflows. All require operational ownership beyond writing a task.

picks.label: Scheduled task DAGs
picks.reason: A mature DAG model and operator ecosystem suit scheduled batch pipelines.
picks.tradeoff: A production deployment has several services and scheduling concepts.

picks.label: Python flow control
picks.reason: Python flows and task state help add orchestration around existing Python work.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted services and self-managed deployments have different operations and pricing.

picks.label: Data-asset modeling
picks.reason: Asset-oriented orchestration makes produced datasets and dependencies visible.
picks.tradeoff: Adopting the asset model may require restructuring existing pipelines.

picks.label: Declarative event workflows
picks.reason: YAML workflow definitions and plugins connect jobs across systems.
picks.tradeoff: Plugin behavior and edition-specific capabilities need review.

recipes.title: Publish business intelligence reports
recipes.description: Distinguish browser-built dashboards from reports maintained as source code. Hosting, authentication and advanced governance may belong to a separate edition.

picks.label: Accessible browser exploration
picks.reason: A query and dashboard interface helps teams explore connected data.
picks.tradeoff: Embedding and governance features can be edition-dependent.

picks.label: Configurable analytical dashboards
picks.reason: SQL exploration, charts and dashboards fit an administered BI service.
picks.tradeoff: Deployment and semantic configuration require technical ownership.

picks.label: Reports as reviewed code
picks.reason: SQL, Markdown and reusable components suit versioned analytical reports.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted Studio capabilities are separate from the Core framework.

recipes.title: Choose a project test runner
recipes.description: Start with the language and build system. These runners belong to different ecosystems; compare features only after choosing the relevant ecosystem.

picks.label: Python tests and fixtures
picks.reason: Fixtures, assertions and plugins fit Python projects.
picks.tradeoff: Plugin compatibility and fixture design need maintenance.

picks.label: Vite-aligned JavaScript tests
picks.reason: A test runner integrated with the Vite ecosystem can share project configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Existing Jest behavior should be checked during migration.

picks.label: Established JavaScript suites
picks.reason: A broad JavaScript testing ecosystem supports existing Jest-based projects.
picks.tradeoff: Module-system and transformer configuration can be involved.

picks.label: Shell command behavior
picks.reason: Bash-based tests can assert command output and exit status.
picks.tradeoff: Shell portability still needs testing on the actual target environments.

recipes.title: Check code and automation files before running them
recipes.description: Use a checker that understands the file language. Static findings are useful evidence, but passing a linter does not establish runtime correctness or security.

picks.label: Python linting and formatting
picks.reason: Python-focused lint rules and formatting provide a combined local code-quality tool.
picks.tradeoff: Rule configuration and unsafe fixes require deliberate review.

picks.label: Shell-script diagnostics
picks.reason: Shell-aware analysis catches quoting and portability issues.
picks.tradeoff: It cannot validate every runtime input or external command.

picks.label: Dockerfile checks
picks.reason: Dockerfile rules and shell analysis support container build-file review.
picks.tradeoff: Image behavior and vulnerability status require separate checks.

picks.label: GitHub Actions definitions
picks.reason: Workflow syntax and expression checking catch errors before a hosted run.
picks.tradeoff: External action behavior and credentials are outside static validation.

recipes.title: Transform developer data locally
recipes.description: Compare isolated utility widgets with a chained transformation workflow. Confirm whether the chosen deployment executes data processing locally before using sensitive input.

picks.label: Individual developer utilities
picks.reason: A collection of encoders, converters and generators covers many small tasks.
picks.tradeoff: A selected hosted instance is distinct from self-hosting the application.

picks.label: Repeatable transformation recipes
picks.reason: Composable operations make decoding and conversion sequences inspectable.
picks.tradeoff: Recipes need validation against the actual input format; a successful decode is not proof of meaning.

recipes.title: Evaluate language-model applications
recipes.description: Separate automated evaluation from observing production traces and collecting human review data. Model-based scores need validation against the task you care about.

picks.label: Automated evaluation cases
picks.reason: A test-oriented evaluation library helps define repeatable checks for LLM behavior.
picks.tradeoff: Judge models, metric settings and API costs can affect results.

picks.label: Traces and evaluation context
picks.reason: Observability connects prompts, model calls and evaluation records.
picks.tradeoff: Running the platform and handling telemetry data require operational choices.

picks.label: Human review datasets
picks.reason: Configurable labeling interfaces support human evaluation tasks.
picks.tradeoff: Annotation design and reviewer agreement remain part of the methodology.

recipes.title: Label vision and text datasets
recipes.description: Select for annotation modality, export format and reviewer workflow. Verify what the self-hosted edition includes before assuming a hosted demo represents it.

picks.label: Visual annotation workflows
picks.reason: Image, video and point-cloud tools plus standard exports fit computer-vision labeling.
picks.tradeoff: Community requires an operated server and differs from Online and Enterprise.

picks.label: Configurable multi-modal tasks
picks.reason: Templates and configurable labeling interfaces adapt to varied annotation work.
picks.tradeoff: Complex workflows can require custom configuration and integration.

picks.label: Text and model feedback
picks.reason: Dataset fields and a Python SDK connect text review to programmatic workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Upstream limits ongoing work to maintenance rather than new feature development.

recipes.title: Transcribe media on your computer
recipes.description: Local inference requires the appropriate model files and hardware. Check language and audio quality on your own sample; no accuracy ranking is established here.

picks.label: Desktop transcription and subtitles
picks.reason: A GUI, watch folders and subtitle exports suit repeated media workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Choose the correct published architecture; v1.4.5 remains the last Intel Mac package.

picks.label: Scriptable local inference
picks.reason: A native implementation supports CLI and embedded transcription workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Model conversion, runtime options and integrations take technical setup.

recipes.title: Install and maintain game modlists
recipes.description: Start with the exact game and mod ecosystem. A modlist manager cannot promise compatibility between arbitrary lists or replace the author’s installation instructions.

picks.label: Curated list installations
picks.reason: Automated list installation helps reproduce an author-defined supported setup.
picks.tradeoff: Downloads, game versions and required third-party accounts must match the list.

picks.label: Thunderstore game profiles
picks.reason: Profiles and dependency handling fit supported Thunderstore communities.
picks.tradeoff: It does not cover every game or mod distribution site.

recipes.title: Choose a game mod loader
recipes.description: The game and runtime decide which loader is applicable. These are ecosystem-specific foundations rather than interchangeable tools for every game.

picks.label: Stardew Valley mods
picks.reason: A game-specific API and loader connect supported Stardew Valley mods.
picks.tradeoff: Game and mod versions must be compatible with the installed SMAPI release.

picks.label: Supported Unity games
picks.reason: A loader and framework support mods for compatible Unity runtimes.
picks.tradeoff: Compatibility varies by game and anti-cheat or online policy.

picks.label: Executable-specific mod setups
picks.reason: A launcher and loader organize configurations for supported PC games.
picks.tradeoff: Each mod and game has its own setup and compatibility requirements.

recipes.title: Organize an emulation library
recipes.description: Distinguish a frontend that launches other software from a framework that also manages emulator cores. Neither provides game files or guarantees a particular game runs.

picks.label: Configured desktop collection
picks.reason: A desktop frontend organizes game metadata, themes and launch commands.
picks.tradeoff: Emulators and legally obtained game files must be configured separately; Android terms differ.

picks.label: Theme-driven launcher
picks.reason: A customizable frontend can unify games and applications under metadata definitions.
picks.tradeoff: Theme and launch configuration take manual work.

picks.label: Core-based emulation interface
picks.reason: A shared frontend provides settings and controls across supported emulator cores.
picks.tradeoff: Compatibility depends on the selected core and its requirements.

recipes.title: Inspect graphics API frames
recipes.description: Select by graphics API, operating system and GPU. Capturing a frame is a development or debugging workflow, not a promise to increase frame rate.

picks.label: Cross-vendor frame capture
picks.reason: A frame debugger exposes graphics API calls and resources on supported APIs.
picks.tradeoff: Supported APIs and capture environments must match the application.

picks.label: Trace and replay API calls
picks.reason: Trace/replay tools help inspect a sequence of graphics calls.
picks.tradeoff: The workflow and API coverage differ from a full vendor profiler.

picks.label: DirectX on Windows
picks.reason: Microsoft’s tooling supports DirectX analysis on Windows.
picks.tradeoff: Its platform and API scope are specific; licensing was not fully classified.

picks.label: NVIDIA graphics analysis
picks.reason: Vendor tooling provides graphics debugging and profiling for supported NVIDIA hardware.
picks.tradeoff: Driver, GPU and API requirements must be checked.

recipes.title: Choose a build orchestrator
recipes.description: Build graphs, language rules and cache infrastructure matter more than a generic speed claim. Compare using the project’s real dependency graph.

picks.label: Explicit multi-language build graph
picks.reason: Declared targets and toolchains support cached and reproducible build workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Rule ecosystems and dependency declarations require investment.

picks.label: Large dependency-graph workflows
picks.reason: A modern build engine targets incremental execution and programmable rules.
picks.tradeoff: Adoption requires compatible rules, toolchains and project migration.

picks.label: Python-defined builds
picks.reason: Python build descriptions fit projects needing programmable build logic.
picks.tradeoff: Its execution and cache model differ from remote-build-oriented systems.

recipes.title: Run a local web development stack
recipes.description: Decide whether the project primarily needs containers with web services or a shell containing language tools. Docker-provider terms and resource use remain separate.

picks.label: PHP and CMS development
picks.reason: Documented local HTTPS, databases, Xdebug and quickstarts support common CMS projects.
picks.tradeoff: Requires a supported Docker provider and is primarily a development environment.

picks.label: Custom service recipes
picks.reason: A Landofile combines application recipes, services and project commands.
picks.tradeoff: Plugins and Docker configuration must match the team environment.

picks.label: Toolchain-oriented shell
picks.reason: A JSON declaration installs project tools through Nix.
picks.tradeoff: It does not automatically provide the same container-service topology.

recipes.title: Choose project environment control
recipes.description: Variable loading, tool installation and reproducible package builds are separate layers. Several of these tools can be used together.

picks.label: Automatic project variables
picks.reason: Approved environment settings load and unload with directory changes.
picks.tradeoff: It executes authorized shell code and does not install a full toolchain itself.

picks.label: Declared tools with simpler configuration
picks.reason: A JSON package list creates a Nix-backed project shell.
picks.tradeoff: Package behavior and Windows WSL requirements still apply.

picks.label: Detailed package and build control
picks.reason: Declarative dependency models support reproducible shells and custom packages.
picks.tradeoff: Its packaging language and store model take more learning.

picks.label: Language tool versions and tasks
picks.reason: A project-oriented manager coordinates common developer tool versions and tasks.
picks.tradeoff: Backend and tool-specific installation behavior needs checking.

recipes.title: Build a data-driven internal app
recipes.description: Choose around the main artifact: editable database records, an analytical report, or a visually assembled application. Authentication and database access remain explicit design work.

picks.label: SQL-defined forms and pages
picks.reason: Queries can produce data-entry forms, tables and charts with a small server.
picks.tradeoff: Application permissions and validation must be designed carefully.

picks.label: Analytical narrative and metrics
picks.reason: SQL and Markdown reports combine explanation with reusable analytical components.
picks.tradeoff: It is report-oriented; Studio features have separate scope.

picks.label: Visual application assembly
picks.reason: Widgets and data connections support internal tool interfaces.
picks.tradeoff: Edition limits and the hosted/self-managed deployment model must fit the project.

recipes.title: Choose an integrated JavaScript runtime
recipes.description: Evaluate an existing application, its native dependencies and deployment target before replacing a runtime. This is a documented-feature comparison, not a universal speed ranking.

picks.label: Explicit permissions and TypeScript tooling
picks.reason: Runtime permissions and built-in development commands suit controlled TypeScript execution.
picks.tradeoff: Node compatibility and permission settings need testing on the actual application.

picks.label: Runtime plus package and build tools
picks.reason: A single toolkit combines JavaScript execution, dependencies, bundling and tests.
picks.tradeoff: Check Node/native-module compatibility and the required CPU/platform build.

recipes.title: Manage JavaScript project dependencies
recipes.description: Package-manager choice affects lockfiles, install scripts and CI behavior. Keep one deliberate project policy and validate changes with the actual dependency tree.

picks.label: Standard Node package workflow
picks.reason: The bundled CLI offers package scripts, workspaces and locked CI installation.
picks.tradeoff: Registry services have separate terms from the open-source CLI.

picks.label: Shared package-store workflow
picks.reason: A content-addressed store and workspace tooling suit many multi-project setups.
picks.tradeoff: Dependencies that assume a flat installation may need fixes.

picks.label: Configurable resolution and workspaces
picks.reason: Modern Yarn offers plugins, constraints and Plug’n’Play or node_modules strategies.
picks.tradeoff: Modern Yarn and Classic differ; migration needs compatibility checks.

picks.label: Integrated toolkit adoption
picks.reason: Its package manager can be evaluated alongside the runtime and test tools.
picks.tradeoff: Adopting one component does not prove the entire toolkit fits a project.

recipes.title: Choose a version-control working style
recipes.description: Compare a new change model, a conventional Git GUI and a complete repository/project system. Their storage and collaboration semantics differ.

picks.label: Git-backed change editing
picks.reason: Automatic snapshots, operation history and descendant rebasing suit stacked-change workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Higher-level metadata and bookmark semantics differ from ordinary Git.

picks.label: Conventional Git with a GUI
picks.reason: Diff, staging and history controls work on ordinary local Git repositories.
picks.tradeoff: It changes the interface rather than replacing Git’s underlying model.

picks.label: Integrated project history
picks.reason: Source control, tickets, wiki and forum can travel in one self-hosted system.
picks.tradeoff: The repository format and collaboration workflow differ from Git.

recipes.title: Back up PC game saves
recipes.description: Choose discovery and automation separately, verify a representative restore, and keep a backup copy outside the original disk. Neither application guarantees every game’s save format transfers between systems.

picks.label: Cross-store scan and portable backups
picks.reason: A game manifest, custom entries and a CLI support manual or scripted save backups.
picks.tradeoff: Verify detected paths and restore behavior for each important game.

picks.label: Backup after game exit
picks.reason: Process monitoring can create compressed save history after playing.
picks.tradeoff: Supported process definitions and paths must be configured; macOS is not documented.

recipes.title: Adjust a game’s rendering workflow
recipes.description: Choose by the exact visual problem and supported game/API. Review multiplayer and anti-cheat restrictions before using injected tools.

picks.label: Presentation, HDR and pacing controls
picks.reason: A game modification framework exposes HDR, display and frame-pacing adjustments.
picks.tradeoff: Per-game compatibility and stable/experimental differences matter; no general speed gain is promised.

picks.label: Post-processing shaders
picks.reason: A shader injector supports a customizable post-processing pipeline.
picks.tradeoff: Game/API compatibility and online restrictions still apply.
